item.title: What Bangladesh can gain from PM's Japan visit
item.description:
The upcoming visit of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to Japan presents a significant opportunity to strengthen Bangladesh's economic potential and international partnerships. According to government statements, the primary focus of this visit, scheduled for 26 October, is bilateral relations, economic partnerships, and investment. To transform these expectations into sustainable achievements, clear preparation and consistent implementation are necessary.

The foundation of this relationship was established during the post-independence reconstruction period. On 10 February 1972, Japan recognised Bangladesh, and diplomatic relations were established. Since then, the continuity of relationships and cooperation has been maintained during various governments. This five-decade trust is a valuable diplomatic asset for Bangladesh.

Collaboration on projects like the Jamuna Multipurpose Bridge, Japanese financing, and technical involvement in Dhaka's metro rail and Jamuna railway bridge have significantly contributed to the communication system. The Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B) initiative in 2014 unveiled the integrated potential of infrastructure, industry, and regional connectivity. Matarbari and Araihazar are the foundations for expanding that cooperation. Evaluating the achievements of existing projects and the potential of ongoing initiatives can enhance production, employment, and local businesses.

Prime Minister to visit Japan tomorrow, raising hopes for fresh investment momentum

The first priority could be preparing to leverage the benefits of the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) signed on 6 February 2026. Joint action plans on essential processes for implementing the agreement, tariff regulations, rules of origin, certification, and customs procedures are required. Guidelines for small and medium exporters and training for officials will be helpful. Besides garments, market research can be conducted on leather goods, processed food, and light engineering sectors. To transform market advantages into sustainable trade, standards, punctuality, and consistent supply are essential.

In investment discussions, specific proposals, including prepared land, electricity, water, transport connections, and approval systems, could be fruitful. Based on the Araihazar Economic Zone, feasibility studies on machinery, electrical equipment, packaging, and food processing can be conducted. Encouraging joint ventures among Japanese medium-sized enterprises and Bangladeshi entrepreneurs, considering local suppliers, skilled workers, and market demand, is essential alongside large corporations.

Administrative reliability will support these efforts. A system for resolving investors' issues within a specified timeframe can increase predictability in approvals, tariff applications, and financial transactions. If the benefits of similar reforms reach domestic businesses as well, the overall investment environment will improve.

Ambassador to stay away from Tokyo during PM's Japan visit, ministry secretary sent to coordinate

In infrastructure cooperation, connecting the development of Matarbari Port and the Maheshkhali-Matarbari area with roads, railways, warehouses, customs, and industrial zones is crucial. Joint initiatives to reduce the time and cost of goods transportation through digital customs, risk-based inspections, operational training, and information exchange can be undertaken. Considering loan terms, foreign currency repayment obligations, usage, and maintenance expenses in new projects will enhance the economic sustainability of cooperation.

Collaboration with Japanese partners on joint research and practical training with universities, polytechnics, and industrial enterprises will be beneficial in this regard. Cooperation can be increased in machinery maintenance, quality control, water management, and disaster-resilient construction. Alongside technology acquisition, capabilities in management, repair, and adaptation to local needs must be developed.

In human resource collaboration, the 2019 framework on skilled workers needs to be more effectively linked with the practical needs of employers. Joint curricula could emphasise language and technical training, comprehensible employment contracts, cost transparency, prevention of unscrupulous mediation, and grievance resolution. With an increase in worker numbers, equal importance must be given to improving skills, income, and protection.

The long-term goal should be to enrich the country's production and knowledge base alongside overseas employment. Training in Japanese institutions, joint factories in Bangladesh, and opportunities for returning workers to become entrepreneurs can be integrated into a single plan. The recognition of qualifications, research environment, and investment facilities will encourage voluntary return and the dissemination of skills within the country. This will extend the benefits of migration beyond remittances.

Bangladesh's industrial history provides significant examples in this context. In the late 1970s, the country's garment sector spread production and management knowledge across the clothing industry with the assistance of trained workers and South Korea's Daewoo. This experience shows that the enduring achievements of international cooperation lie in the learning capabilities of people and institutions. In the current partnership, it is essential to consider what skills remain in the country after a project's completion.

Collaboration with Japanese partners on joint research and practical training with universities, polytechnics, and industrial enterprises will be beneficial in this regard. Cooperation can be increased in machinery maintenance, quality control, water management, and disaster-resilient construction. Alongside technology acquisition, capabilities in management, repair, and adaptation to local needs must be developed.

PM's Japan visit to prioritise economic partnership, investment: Humaiun

In environment and energy sectors, the cooperation memorandum of February 2026 can be utilised to assess opportunities for energy savings, waste management, rooftop solar power, and disaster preparedness in industries. Considering local capability and long-term operational costs, choosing initiatives will reduce production costs and environmental risks.
These Japan-focused initiatives need to be part of Bangladesh's integrated East Asia strategy. The production and supply network of China, Japan's industrial technology, and quality management, combined with South Korea's production and technology experience, can be coordinated with Bangladesh's priorities.

Bangladesh's strategic position of development-centric autonomy can be useful. Recognising the unique value of each relationship, mutual trust, national interests, and freedom of decision-making must be maintained. Closer cooperation with Japan and close ties with China can create complementary developmental opportunities. Common standards in loan sustainability, transparent procurement processes, information security, environment, and effective state control over critical infrastructure will make this position credible.

Utilising its location in the Bay of Bengal, Bangladesh can be an effective connector between the markets of South Asia and the production systems of East Asia. For this, along with integrated transportation and customs, mutually agreed trade systems with neighbours are necessary. If local production, repair services, research, and suppliers are developed, the benefits of the connection will remain within the country. Diversity in financing, technology, and import sources will also increase economic resilience.

In a five to ten-year East Asia cooperation plan, priority industries, supplier capabilities, training, joint research, and production stages can be determined. Opportunities for local procurement and learning on mutually agreeable terms need to be increased. Indicators of evaluation will be realistic investment, domestic value addition, worker income, local orders, and technical capabilities.

There are opportunities to expand cooperation in maritime security, disaster assistance, international law, and peaceful dispute resolution. Japan's consistent diplomatic involvement is expected in creating a conducive environment for humanitarian aid for the Rohingya and for safe, voluntary, and dignified repatriation.

After the visit, publishing an implementation list with responsible agencies, timelines, and a review process will be helpful. In the six-month and one-year progress assessments, announced investments, actual cash flow and production, and training and employment need to be considered separately. Five decades of trust can be the foundation for the next decade's industrialisation if production is linked with infrastructure and knowledge is intertwined with migration.

item.title: Six shipments of LNG being purchased from Singapore and Qatar
item.description:
The cabinet committee on government purchase has approved a proposal to purchase five cargoes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Singapore-based BP Singapore Pte. Ltd. and one cargo from Qatar Energy Trading LLC.

The prices set for the purchase of the six LNG cargoes are lower than the international market’s Japan-Korea Marker (JKM) index.

The proposal was approved at a meeting of the cabinet committee on government purchase held yesterday, Saturday. The Ministry of Finance announced the decision in a press release today, Sunday.

According to the press release, LNG will be purchased from BP Singapore at a price of $0.17 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) below the JKM index.

Meanwhile, a proposal to purchase an additional LNG cargo from Qatar Energy Trading LLC under a long-term contract has been approved. In this case, the price has been set at $0.10 per MMBtu below the JKM index.

Separately, at the 33rd meeting of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, the Energy and Mineral Resources Division presented a proposal to purchase LNG from JERA Global Markets Pte. Ltd. through the direct procurement method.

Under Section 68 of the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and Rule 99(2) of the Public Procurement Rules, 2025, the proposal called for direct negotiations with the company and the signing of a short-term LNG sale and purchase agreement (SPA) and a term sheet.

According to the press release, it was decided that the proposal would be presented at the next meeting after vetting by the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division.

item.title: Govt defers proposal to buy LNG from JERAGM pending legal vetting
item.description:
The government has deferred a proposal seeking approval to purchase liquefied natural gas (LNG) directly from Japan’s JERA Global Markets Pte Ltd (JERAGM), pending legal vetting by the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division.
The decision was taken at the 35th meeting of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs held on Saturday, where a single proposal from the Energy and Mineral Resources Division was placed for discussion.
Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury presided over the meeting.
The proposal sought approval in principle to procure LNG from JERAGM through the direct procurement method under Section 68 of the Public Procurement Act, 2006, and Rule 99(2) of the Public Procurement Rules, 2025.
It also sought approval to sign the finalised formats of the short-term LNG Sale and Purchase Agreement (SPA) and the term sheet between Bangladesh Oil, Gas and Mineral Corporation (Petrobangla) and JERAGM.
The committee decided that the proposal will be placed before it again after obtaining vetting from the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division.
No final approval for the proposed LNG purchase or signing of the agreements was granted at the meeting.

item.title: Shama Obaed to visit Spain, UK to boost trade and cultural ties
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam leaves on Monday on an official visit to Spain and the United Kingdom to deepen economic partnerships and expand cultural cooperation.
During the visit, scheduled for October 26-30, she will meet dignitaries to explore cooperation in trade, investment, tourism, skills development and cultural exchange, said a foreign ministry press release on Sunday.
The visit will begin in Seville, Spain, where she will inaugurate the third Spain-Bangladesh Expo 2026 on October 26.
Organized by the Spain-Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SBCCI), the expo will be held under the theme "Stronger Partnership, Shared Prosperity".
The event aims to connect Bangladeshi exporters with Spanish manufacturers, importers and investors, opening avenues for trade and investment partnerships.
Following her engagements in Spain, Shama will visit the United Kingdom on October 29-30.
Her UK engagements will focus on promoting Bangladeshi art and culture, expanding international cultural partnerships and exploring opportunities to develop Bangladesh's creative economy.
The visit reflects Bangladesh's commitment to advancing economic diplomacy, attracting investment and strengthening cultural cooperation with European partners, the release said.

You’ll amend the constitution, only for it to be whitewashed in court—we don’t agree: Jamaat Ameer
item.description:
Opposition Leader and Ameer of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, Shafiqur Rahman, has urged the government to step back from amending the constitution.

“Will you pass just another amendment? A court will completely whitewash it... We are not accustomed to, nor do we agree to, engaging in such futile efforts and persisting with the mistaken approaches of the past. That is precisely why we demand reform,” he stated.

Shafiqur Rahman made these remarks while delivering his presidential address at a discussion organised by Jamaat-e-Islami at the Kazi Nazrul Islam Auditorium of the National Press Club in the capital on Sunday afternoon, marking the anniversary of the signing of the July National Charter.

Addressing the ruling party, the Jamaat ameer said, “Why are you searching for the constitution now? To search for the constitution, you spent 15 and a half years holding a few meetings and rallies with the gracious permission of the government. Yet, you could not oust fascism. Neither could we, nor could you. That is the reality.”

The Opposition Leader alleged that upon coming to power, BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) forgot the past.

Shafiqur Rahman remarked that the government must break free from its mindset of amending the constitution. He stated that this constitution not only birthed fascism but also sought to give fascism a permanent structure.

Shafiqur Rahman criticised the BNP’s stance on implementing the July National Charter. He noted that the BNP had expressed objections to significant reform proposals by issuing “notes of dissent”. Now, even the matters to which they had no objections are being evaded.

The Jamaat ameer claimed that the BNP did not take a stance in favour of a “Yes” vote in the referendum. Instead, the party’s cadres both at home and abroad were instructed to vote “No”. However, that attempt failed due to the public verdict.

Shafiqur Rahman expressed criticism over inviting the Opposition to discussions within the committee formed to amend the constitution. He remarked that they (the ruling party) had betrayed 70 per cent of the populace. The Opposition would not do that. The government will be compelled to implement this referendum.

The Jamaat ameer also accused BNP of entering into an electoral understanding with Awami League (whose activities are banned in the country).

He stated that during the election, BNP subtly begged for votes from Awami League. Sheikh Hasina and a godfather of the Awami League both mentioned this. A BNP Member of Parliament (MP) from Natore even thanked Awami League members for their success in the election.

He further alleged that leaders from various organisations, including the Awami League, Jubo League, and Chhatra League, were given prominent positions within the BNP.

Shafiqur Rahman raised questions regarding the law and order situation in the country. He asserted that if the government cannot prevent the influx of money, weapons, and drugs across the borders, it lacks the qualification to govern the country.

The Opposition Leader noted that while the government announces various types of cards on one hand, people's lives have become miserable due to the burden of taxes and corruption on the other. The government lacks effective plans to rehabilitate returnee expatriates and restore comfort to the lives of ordinary citizens.

The Jamaat ameer remarked that the prices of daily essentials are soaring due to extortion and illegal occupation. He cited that in Panchagarh, farmers sell four gourds for one taka, whereas consumers in Dhaka are forced to purchase a single gourd for 40 to 60 taka.

Referring to the incident of attack, vandalism, and looting at the Radda MCH-FP Centre, a private maternal and child health clinic in Mirpur, Dhaka, Shafiqur Rahman stressed that the resignation of the concerned MP is not enough; she must be brought to justice under the law.

Shafiqur Rahman also accused the government of subtly attempting to shift the blame onto the Opposition in an effort to cover up its monumental failures.

Criticising the government’s anxiety regarding the Opposition’s programmes, Shafiqur Rahman asked why the government is so perturbed by the long march if it truly believes the programme lacks public support.

He called on the government not to obstruct the Opposition’s activities or attempt to impose chaos upon them.

The Jamaat ameer remarked that he has no objection if the prime minister consumes a lunch worth 100 to 150 taka. However, the government must ensure arrangements so that ordinary citizens can comfortably afford two square meals a day and live in peace.

Speaking at the discussion, President of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), Colonel (retd) Oli Ahmad, said that Tarique Rahman must take lessons from the past.

However, he warned that it is the people around the prime minister who will cause his downfall, and the prime minister cannot emerge victorious while fighting battles on all fronts.

He urged the immediate announcement of the implementation of the July Charter in the public interest.

Akhter Hossen, Member Secretary of the National Citizen Party (NCP), alleged that despite the legal foundation of the July Charter and the verdict of the referendum, the government wishes to reject the reform proposals.

He stated that they (the BNP) now refuse to comply even with the proposals they previously agreed to, adding that the BNP has no desire to implement any reform agenda and is instead seeking pretexts to retreat.

THe senior NCP leader asserted that the crisis must be resolved by dissolving the one-sided, single-party constitutional amendment committee and establishing a constitutional reform council in line with the referendum mandate.

Mia Golam Porwar, Secretary General of Jamaat, remarked that the ground beneath the government’s feet has slipped away. Consequently, they are uttering nonsense and attempting to cling to power by misleading the nation.

He added that an ill-fated attempt is being made to amend the constitution under the guise of a special committee, creating new narratives that run contrary to the spirit of the July Charter.

Among others who addressed the discussion were Jamaat Nayeb-e-Ameer Mujeebur Rahman, Assistant Secretary General Hamidur Rahman Azad, Central Executive Council members Saiful Alam Khan (Milon), Nurul Islam Bulbul, and Salim Uddin; Jamaat Working Council member Shishir Monir; former diplomat Sakib Ali; AB Party Secretary Asaduzzaman Fuaad; President of Nexus Defence and Justice, Brigadier General (retd) Md. Hasan Nasir; retired army officer Hasinur Rahman; former DUJ President Elahi Newaz Khan; DUJ President Shahidul Islam; lawyer ASM Shahriar Kabir; and reserved seat MP and mother of July martyr Jabir Ibrahim, Rokeya Begum.

item.title: The mistake keeping Bangladesh from tapping into Japan’s labour market
item.description:
Japan’s labour shortage, driven by its ageing population, has created a major opportunity for Bangladesh. However, we have fallen behind due to gaps in skills, Japanese-language proficiency and demand-driven training.

By measuring labour migration in terms of numbers rather than skills, failing to formulate effective policies and plan ahead, and being unable to build effective partnerships with employers, we have failed to turn our demographic advantage into sustainable employment despite having a large young population.

There are several clear examples of Bangladesh’s past failures in accessing Japan’s labour market. In July 2005, an agreement between Bangladesh and Japan was signed to create opportunities for Bangladeshi workers to receive technical training and work in Japan. However, over the following eight years, Bangladesh managed to send only 41 workers to Japan under the agreement, 12 through the government agency, the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET), and 29 through private recruitment agencies.

This was an embarrassing example of policy failure on Bangladesh’s part. Yet Japanese small and medium-sized enterprises had a demand for Bangladeshi workers. Inadequate language skills, inappropriate worker selection, lengthy administrative procedures and a lack of coordination among the organisations concerned stood in the way of capitalising on that opportunity. Our failure to move forward was not due to a lack of opportunities, but rather an inability to turn those opportunities into actual employment.

Although an agreement was reached with Japan’s IM Japan in 2015 to train 500 Bangladeshis, and a new initiative was launched in 2017 to provide one-year training in the manufacturing and construction sectors, Bangladesh failed to demonstrate the capacity to turn these initiatives into large-scale, sustained employment programmes.

Even after Bangladesh signed a memorandum of cooperation with Japan on a framework for sending Specified Skilled Workers (SSW) on August 27, 2019, overcoming limitations in language education, skills assessment and transparent recruitment has remained an urgent priority.

More significantly, surveys conducted by Japan’s immigration authorities among technical trainees from various countries have revealed that many fall into debt after paying large sums of money to recruitment agencies and intermediaries in their home countries. In light of this risk, Bangladesh’s failure to establish a transparent and accountable recruitment system needs to be reassessed.

These experiences demonstrate that signing a memorandum of understanding is not, in itself, a measure of success. True success lies in translating such agreements into skilled workers, lower migration costs and sustainable employment.

What Bangladesh can gain from PM's Japan visit

First mistake: Training before demand, investment without job guarantees

One of the major weaknesses of Bangladesh’s labour export system is the disconnect between training and actual recruitment. Training programmes should be designed based on data showing how many workers are needed in each sector, what qualifications employers require and which skills tests candidates must pass. However, the tendency to measure success by the number of training centres, trainees or certificates issued has obscured the actual outcomes.

Learning Japanese, acquiring professional skills and passing qualification tests are time-consuming processes. When training centres vary in quality and there are no genuine employment opportunities after training, young people end up wasting both time and money. As a result, many aspiring to work in Japan fall behind even at the preparation stage.

The question is: why has Bangladesh not done enough to establish partnerships with Japanese employers and introduce training programmes tailored to their needs? Why has the country failed to develop the capacity to assess demand in foreign labour markets based on data rather than assumptions?

This failure cannot be attributed to any one individual; it reflects longstanding weaknesses in policymaking and institutional management.

Second Mistake: Failing to treat language as a core skill requirement

Japanese-language proficiency is not merely an additional qualification for working in Japan. It is essential for understanding workplace instructions, communicating with colleagues, maintaining safety and managing daily life. Yet Bangladesh has failed to make the expected progress in establishing a comprehensive system that makes Japanese-language education accessible, affordable and of consistent quality.

The concentration of opportunities in Dhaka, high training costs and a shortage of qualified teachers create barriers for prospective workers. For a young person in a rural area, covering the costs of language classes, examinations and documentation can often be difficult. In other words, in a labour market where preparation is crucial for entry, access to that preparation is not equal for everyone.

The state’s responsibility was not simply to establish training centres, but to integrate language education, vocational training and recruitment into a single system. The absence of such a coordinated approach has put Bangladesh at a disadvantage.

Third mistake: Failing to establish a reliable, low-cost recruitment system

Complaints about intermediaries, opaque fees, fraud and excessive costs have long plagued Bangladesh’s migration system. Preparing to enter a market such as Japan is already expensive. When uncertainty over recruitment is added to the equation, the risks for young workers and their families increase manifold.

Japanese employers, meanwhile, want partners who can reliably provide suitable workers. If Bangladesh cannot ensure transparent recruitment, verified training and reasonable costs, it cannot gain a competitive advantage simply by virtue of its abundant workforce.

Our mistake has been to leave migration largely dependent on individuals’ own initiative and financial capacity. The state, however, should have taken responsibility for controlling recruitment costs, effectively monitoring licensed recruitment agencies and establishing channels for direct engagement with foreign employers. When workers fall into debt before even leaving for a job abroad, much of the benefit of securing higher-paying employment is undermined.

Fourth mistake: Failing to recognise the importance of competitors

Bangladesh is not alone in Japan’s labour market. Other labour-sending countries are also working to expand language education, technical training and cooperation with employers. Some benefit from decades of labour migration experience, established recruitment networks and familiarity with the Japanese language and culture.

Bangladesh’s policymakers should have analysed the experiences of competing countries to identify the country’s own weaknesses. A sustained strategy was needed to determine which sectors offer Bangladesh a comparative advantage, where training needs to be expanded and how employers’ confidence could be earned. However, the complacency associated with being a major labour-sending country prevented us from fully appreciating the importance of such competitive preparation.

What is needed now is accountability, not promises

To overcome these failures, the first step should be to develop a five-year action plan for Japan’s labour market, with measurable targets. Clear indicators must specify how many workers are to be sent to Japan in each sector, how many will receive language and skills training, how many will secure jobs and how many will remain employed. The performance of training institutions must be measured not by the number of certificates issued, but by actual employment outcomes and workers’ earnings.

Direct partnerships must be established with Japanese employers, industry associations and training institutions. At the same time, access to language education and skills testing must be expanded beyond Dhaka, financial assistance for training must be provided, recruitment costs must be fully disclosed, and swift action must be taken against fraud. Employment contracts must clearly specify wages, working hours, accommodation costs and procedures for filing complaints. Bangladeshis working abroad must also have access to legal assistance in Bangla and an effective grievance redress mechanism.

Most importantly, diplomatic visits and memorandums of understanding must not be presented as substitutes for success. Success should be measured by how many Bangladeshis actually secure decent jobs, how little they have to spend to migrate and how safely they can work abroad.
Japan’s labour market presents a major opportunity for Bangladesh, but there is no guarantee that this window of opportunity will remain open indefinitely. Unless we learn from past mistakes, new initiatives will simply repeat old failures. Bangladesh must establish itself not as a source of cheap labour, but as a partner capable of delivering skilled, reliable workers while safeguarding their rights.

The question, therefore, is not merely how many workers Bangladesh can send to Japan. It is whether, having failed for so long to adequately prepare despite the opportunities available, we now have the political will to take responsibility for those failures and correct them.

item.title: Bangladesh eyes $13.8bn investment, more jobs
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman left Dhaka for Tokyo on Sunday on a four-day official visit aimed at expanding trade and investment, creating employment opportunities and increasing exports of skilled workers to Japan.
During the visit, he is scheduled to hold a bilateral summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, meet leading business executives and investors, and visit automobile and energy facilities.
Ahead of the visit, Bangladesh has prepared a proposed investment and cooperation package worth $13.8 billion across 12 priority sectors for 2026-2031. Meanwhile, Japan's private sector plans to invest approximately 1 trillion yen, or $6.35 billion, in Bangladesh over the next five years, according to Reuters, citing Japanese media outlet Nikkei Asia.
The proposed investments cover transport, industrialisation, manufacturing, energy, technology, agriculture, pharmaceuticals, information technology, tourism, and small and medium-sized enterprises.
Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam said discussions would cover cooperation in agriculture, fisheries, human resource development, skills enhancement, civil aviation, marine environmental protection and local government modernisation.
Around eight memorandums of understanding (MoUs) are under discussion, three to four of which could be signed during the visit, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Automobile manufacturing and energy infrastructure are among the major areas of potential Japanese investment.
According to diplomatic sources, Japanese automaker Toyota is planning to invest around $500 million in a vehicle assembly plant in Bangladesh. The project could create opportunities for local companies involved in manufacturing automobile components and cables, while generating employment for engineers and technically skilled workers.
On Thursday, the final day of the visit, Tarique Rahman is scheduled to visit Toyota Motor Corporation's Motomachi Plant in Nagoya. He is also expected to attend a luncheon hosted by Toshimitsu Imai, president and chief executive officer of Toyota Tsusho Corporation, and visit the Toyota Commemorative Museum of Industry and Technology.
Meanwhile, Japanese energy company JERA has proposed developing an LNG terminal and related infrastructure in the Maheshkhali-Matarbari area to help address Bangladesh's industrial gas shortage, diplomatic sources said.
On Tuesday, the prime minister is scheduled to visit JERA's onshore LNG terminal and power plant in Futtsu, Chiba Prefecture. He will also visit the Nittsu Logistics Hub in Ichikawa.
Bangladesh's proposed package includes $3.45 billion for transport and urban connectivity, $3.14 billion for integrated industrial, port and commercial hubs, including Matarbari, and $1.57 billion for manufacturing and electronics.
Another $1.26 billion is proposed for energy and green transition initiatives, while $940 million would go towards climate-resilient infrastructure. The remaining $3.45 billion would cover agriculture, pharmaceuticals, information technology, the blue economy, tourism and small and medium-sized enterprises.
Japan has long supported Bangladesh's infrastructure development, including Dhaka's metro rail, the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and the Matarbari deep-sea port.
The two countries are expected to discuss the costs and loan terms of ongoing projects, including reducing metro rail construction costs, lowering interest rates on Japanese loans and accelerating project implementation.
The visit is also expected to focus on Japan's Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B) initiative, launched in 2014 under then Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe to support Bangladesh's industrialisation, infrastructure development and regional connectivity.
Diplomatic sources said the initiative was being updated around four pillars, reflecting the Bay of Bengal's growing economic and strategic importance.
The first focuses on regional connectivity and integrated logistics, including developing Matarbari's deep-sea port and energy infrastructure as an international trade hub. The plan also aims to improve goods transportation links with India's northeastern states, Nepal and Bhutan.
The second pillar focuses on alternative maritime routes to address natural disasters, international conflicts and global supply chain disruptions. The third emphasises public-private partnerships, business modernisation and reducing administrative barriers to investment. The fourth focuses on regional peace and maritime security.
Japan has already handed over five patrol vessels to the Bangladesh Navy. Discussions may also advance the supply of a modern 35-metre patrol vessel to the Bangladesh Coast Guard, a diplomatic source in Tokyo said.
Bangladesh and Japan signed an Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) in February, creating opportunities to expand trade and investment.
According to the Export Promotion Bureau and Bangladesh Bank, Bangladesh's annual exports to Japan crossed $1 billion for the first time in the 2015-16 fiscal year, rising to $2.8 billion in 2021-22.
Japan is currently Bangladesh's ninth-largest export destination and its second-largest market in Asia.
Although readymade garments dominate exports, Bangladesh has opportunities to increase pharmaceutical and information technology exports. Greater Japanese investment could also help expand exports of products manufactured in Bangladesh.
In a survey by the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO), 73.2% of 57 Japanese companies identified Bangladesh as a priority destination for business expansion, while 61% cited its strong growth potential.
The Bangladesh Special Economic Zone in Araihazar, Narayanganj, developed with Japanese cooperation and involving Sumitomo Corporation and other partners, could also attract further investment.
Sending skilled and semi-skilled workers to Japan is another key priority.
In August 2019, Bangladesh and Japan signed a memorandum of cooperation to recruit Bangladeshi workers in 14 sectors under Japan's Specified Skilled Worker (SSW) programme. In May 2025, the two countries agreed to recruit at least 100,000 Bangladeshi workers over the following five years.
On October 17, the countries signed another five-year memorandum of cooperation on employment and skills development, which is automatically renewable for a further five years. The initiative aims to expand recruitment opportunities from April 1, 2027.
Technical training, Japanese-language education and professional qualifications will be important in preparing workers for Japan's labour market.
Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam said human resource development and skills enhancement would feature in discussions during the visit. Separate MoUs on education and human resource development are also scheduled.
On Monday, Tarique Rahman is scheduled to meet Taro Aso, president of the Japan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship League, Masumi Kakinoki, chairman of the Japan-Bangladesh Committee for Commercial and Economic Cooperation, and Dr Akihiko Tanaka, president of the Japan International Cooperation Agency.
On Tuesday, he will hold a summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, followed by a joint press conference. Discussions are expected to cover bilateral relations, trade, investment, infrastructure and regional and international issues.
On Wednesday, the prime minister is scheduled to meet Kazuhiko Amakawa, governor of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation, and visit Uniqlo's headquarters to meet its president and board members.
He will also meet JETRO President Susumu Kataoka and representatives of Mitsui & Co, Sumitomo Corporation and JERA. Two group meetings are planned with representatives of 14 additional Japanese companies.
The prime minister will deliver the keynote address at the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum in Tokyo, where business leaders and investors from both countries are expected to discuss trade expansion and new investment opportunities.
On Thursday, he will visit Toyota's facilities before returning to Dhaka via Tokyo. He is scheduled to arrive at 10:35pm on Thursday.
His delegation includes his wife, Dr Zubaida Rahman; Finance Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury; Finance and Planning Adviser Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir; State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir; State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Anindya Islam Amit; Adviser to the Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology Division Rehan Asif Asad; BIDA Chairman Ashik Chowdhury; and the prime minister's Special Assistant Md Shakirul Islam Khan, along with government officials and media representatives.

item.title: SC publishes full verdict on 32,000 primary headteachers’ recruitment dispute
item.description:
The Supreme Court’s Appellate Division has published the full text of its verdict allowing the state’s appeal against a High Court ruling that partially favoured teachers of nationalised primary schools, resolving a long-standing legal dispute involving around 32,000 government primary school headteachers.
The 29-page verdict was published on Sunday, October 25. A four-member Appellate Division bench headed by the chief justice delivered the verdict on July 2.
Following the verdict, Attorney General Md Ruhul Quddus Kazal said the ruling had resolved the legal complications surrounding the recruitment of around 32,000 headteachers at government primary schools. He also expressed hope that the decision would have a positive impact on primary education.
According to case records, teachers of formerly private primary schools brought under government control filed a writ petition with the High Court in 2017, seeking seniority based on counting 50% of their previous service, placement on a gradation list, the salary scale applicable to headteachers, and various financial and administrative benefits.
After the initial hearing, the High Court issued a rule. On March 11, 2019, following the final hearing, it partially upheld the petition and declared part of Rule 9(1) of the Nationalised Primary School Teachers (Terms of Service) Rules, 2013 illegal. The state challenged the ruling before the Appellate Division. On November 20, 2022, the court granted leave to appeal and stayed the operation of the High Court verdict.
The state filed an appeal in 2023, while teachers directly recruited to government primary schools also filed applications before the Appellate Division.
After hearing the appeals, the court ruled in favour of the state on July 2.
The rules governing the terms of service of teachers at nationalised primary schools were introduced on September 29, 2013. Before the nationalisation process, a committee had initially selected 26,193 private primary schools for consideration.

item.title: Body of Bangladeshi man killed in Latvia returns home
item.description:
The body of Bangladeshi national Sohel Rana, who died in Latvia after allegedly being tortured by human traffickers, returned home on Sunday.
The remains of Sohel, 45, son of Abul Hashem, reached his home at Ramchandrapur village in Sadar upazila around 3:00 pm, triggering an outpouring of grief among family members and relatives.
Hundreds of villagers gathered at his home to pay their last respects.
According to his father-in-law, Alfaz Uddin, Sohel was rescued by Latvian police from a forest near the Latvia-Belarus border on October 7 after being subjected to inhuman torture by a human trafficking gang that had promised to send him to Italy.
He died the following day while undergoing treatment at a hospital in Latvia's Latgale region, Alfaz said.
The family was informed of his death through a text message from Polish police on October 12, he added.
On October 17, Sohel's wife, Jasmin Sultana, filed a case with a court accusing nine people in connection with the incident.
The court subsequently directed the Officer-in-Charge of Jhenaidah Sadar Police Station to register the complaint as a first information report (FIR).
Sohel's father, Abul Hashem, said his son's body was brought from Dhaka to their village home after completing the necessary legal procedures and administrative formalities.
Local Union Parishad Chairman Enamul Haque Nilu said Sohel's namaz-e-janaza was held at the local Ramchandrapur School ground in the afternoon, after which he was buried at the family graveyard.
Villagers demanded exemplary punishment for those involved in the alleged human trafficking network responsible for the incident.

item.title: Salahuddin: Govt won’t allow unrest over reported Hasina return in December
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Sunday said the government will not allow anyone to create instability in the country over the reported return of ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in December.
“We are also aware of social media reports that fascist Sheikh Hasina wants to return to Bangladesh in December. However, the government will not allow anyone to create instability in the country over her reported return,” he said.
The minister said Bangladesh has sent several requests to India through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs seeking Hasina’s extradition under the extradition treaty. “Our position is clear here,” he said.
He came up with the information while speaking at a press briefing on the peaceful celebrations of Durga Puja at the Secretariat.
Asked about the law-and-order situation amid discussions over Hasina's possible return in December, he said the forces associated with the previous regime have been attempting to spread misinformation from the beginning.
“They want to create instability in Bangladesh and take advantage of the situation,” Salahuddin said, adding that the government will not allow any anti-state force, fallen political force, fugitive criminal or person accused of genocide to create unrest in the country.
Those who fled the country in the face of the mass uprising and were involved in the killing of hundreds of citizens will not be allowed to carry out subversive activities in Bangladesh, he said.
The minister said the government believed that Durga Puja was celebrated peacefully across Bangladesh after 15 to 17 years, amid enthusiasm and communal harmony.
He expressed gratitude to the Bangladesh Police, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), Bangladesh Ansar and Village Defense Party, intelligence agencies, journalists and people from all walks of life for their cooperation in ensuring peaceful celebrations of the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community.
Salahuddin said incidents of violence, untoward events, terrorist activities and attempts to undermine religious harmony occurred during Durga Puja in the past. “But the country saw no such incidents this year,” he said, expressing hope that the peaceful environment will continue with everyone's cooperation.
He said authorities focused on preventive measures rather than waiting for incidents to occur before taking action.
Using digital systems and various technologies, including mobile apps, authorities monitored the situation from the grassroots through unions, wards, upazilas, districts and divisional centers, with continuous monitoring from the central level, the minister said.
One or two plans to cause incidents around the Durga Puja celebrations were detected in advance, and law enforcement agencies took necessary action accordingly, he said.
Action to be taken about attack on police in Gopalganj
Regarding the attack on police in Gopalganj, Salahuddin said the incident occurred in the Kheyaghat area of a union under Gopalganj Sadar upazila.
Some activists of the Awami League and its associate bodies attempted to organize a procession, he said. “When a police patrol team arrived at the scene, the officers came under attack as they were outnumbered. We have seen the video of the incident. Action is being taken against those involved in the attack,” he said.
Referring to the situation in Sajek, Rangamati, the minister said the law-and-order situation has come under control.
He said several groups operate in the hill region, including the Parbatya Chittagong Jana Samhati Samiti (PCJSS) and the United People's Democratic Front (UPDF), as well as other groups with similar names. “Internal disputes and rivalries exist among these groups,” he added.
Salahuddin said attempts are made every year to gain control over certain areas in the hills during the tourism season.
The government, together with the Bangladesh Army, has taken necessary steps to maintain normalcy and will continue to do so, he said.
The minister added that discussions were also underway with local headmen and community leaders.
The local lawmaker is also maintaining communication with them to help address the situation, he said.

item.title: Saudi Arabia looks to US for an AI edge as Yemen’s Houthis up pressure
item.description:
Under attack from the militant Houthi group in neighboring Yemen, Saudi Arabia has asked numerous allies for help.
That includes the United States, even though media report that US President Donald Trump refused when Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman asked him to take direct military action against the Houthis.
However the US is providing Saudi Arabia with intelligence, which includes a targeting tool that uses artificial intelligence, or AI. A September report by US broadcaster CNN, quoting several unnamed American officials, said that between 100 and 200 US soldiers were in Saudi Arabia as part of new joint force command to facilitate this.
The US personnel were helping the Saudis “use a targeting tool that allows military officers to see in real-time what is happening on the battlefield,” CNN reported.
Officials said the system in Saudi Arabia was similar to that known as the Maven Smart System, or MSS for short, which the US military has also used as it sought targets in Iran, Iraq and Syria.
MSS came out of what’s known as Project Maven, the US’s flagship artificial intelligence program for the military, first launched in 2017. MSS itself is an AI-enabled digital platform that “aggregates, organizes and visualizes vast streams of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance data,” analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington explained in a June text.
The software system identifies patterns in data coming from, for example, live satellite feeds or drone cameras and then labels potential targets such as possible rocket launchers, tanks or suspicious vehicle convoys.
Previously human military analysts would have had to look at a wide array of different sources to try to find those, the CSIS researchers wrote. It was difficult and, in the case of hours of satellite or drone footage, almost impossible. But MSS now brings hundreds of sources together, analyses them all, then flags possible targets. It also calculates the best method of hitting the target.
Tech commentator Bilawal Sidhu, a former Google product manager, has described the MSS set up as like a “Google Earth for war.”
Using the MSS dramatically speeds up what is known as “the kill chain” — that is, the time it takes to detect a target, decide if it’s dangerous and then order a strike.
When the US military used MSS while attacking Iran in late February, the AI-powered system facilitated hits on more than 1,000 targets within the first 24 hours of the war. Previously American soldiers were hitting about 100 targets a day.
Up until recently, the long-simmering civil war in Yemen had been comparatively calm following an informal ceasefire negotiated in 2022.
The Houthi rebel group has held large parts of northern and western Yemen since 2015. Yemen’s internationally recognized government and other groups held territory across the south and east. That latter is supported by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
The Houthi’s latest military campaign, which began in September, has seen the group take further control of Yemen’s coast. They also ramped up attacks against Saudi Arabia again, hitting the country’s main airport and oil facilities. So far, though, military campaigns against the Houthi group by Saudi Arabia, the United States and others have all failed to significantly weaken the group.
This is partially because the Houthis take a “zero-sum approach,” Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow focused on Yemen at UK think tank Chatham House, told DW recently. The group’s founding father argued that contemporary Muslim societies were too “soft,” and that poverty and hardship are a divine test, al-Muslimi said.
“They don’t care if the Israelis bomb the airport or the US bombs a hospital,” she said. “It actually serves them very well because their ideology is all about martyrdom and sacrifice.”
There are certain technical issues users have noted with the MSS in the past that could also prove problematic in Yemen.
The Houthis tend to be highly mobile, using truck-mounted ballistic missiles and small drone swarms as they operate from hills and canyons in rugged countryside. It’s possible that fighters might be long gone before they can be attacked even with the help of AI-assisted targeting.
Though MSS is known to work best in relatively unpopulated areas, factors such as changes in desert terrain, dust storms, high wind, snowfall and dense foliage — and even deliberately planted decoys — can reduce its success rate.
There is also a worrying ethical aspect to shortening the kill chain. A human is always supposed to verify the target that the AI-assisted tool has identified and decide how to react.
But it doesn’t always work that way. For example, among the sites MSS targeted in Iran on the first day of the war was a school. An American missile killed almost 200 people at a primary school in southern Iran, most of them children aged between seven and 12.
In its military campaign in Gaza, Israel — arguably the Middle Eastern country with the most advanced military-use AI — has also used AI-assisted targeting. An Israeli system known as the Gospel, or Habsora, is the closest to MSS in the way it works.
But, as has been documented elsewhere, including by Israeli and British journalists and in the recent documentary Naza, the use of such AI targeting tools have also been highly problematic because of the numbers of civilian casualties that can result.
“On the one hand [in Gaza], AI has enhanced commanders’ situational awareness, lessened the human costs of tunnel mapping, improved the speed of military strikes, and boosted the survivability of troops,” analysts Frederic Wehrey and Andrew Bonney wrote for War on the Rocks, a specialist media outlet. “Yet the benefits afforded by such functions have been overshadowed by mounting civilian deaths reportedly resulting from this technology’s safeguards being loosened or eliminated.”
All of which is why Antony Loewenstein, an independent journalist based in Australia who has researched the impact of Israel’s AI-assisted technology, doesn’t believe similar technology will lead to the defeat of the Houthi group.
“I don’t think there’s much evidence at all that using an AI tool is going to make much difference on the ground, except for causing huge amounts of civilian casualties,” Loewenstein, who authored the book, “The Palestine Laboratory: How Israel Exports The Technology of Occupation Around the World,” told DW. “And I think what the US and the Saudis will find is that the Houthis have an incredibly high tolerance level for destruction.”

item.title: The Thirteenth Mile: This Is What Gray Zone War Looks Like
item.description:
On the morning of October 23, the cargo ship Khoryv sent a distress call 13 nautical miles off Constanța, Romania. Territorial waters end at twelve. Whoever flew the drone that sank her knew where the line was, and chose to stand one mile outside it.

That mile is the story. It is the difference between an attack on a NATO member and an incident in a NATO member's exclusive economic zone. It is the difference between Article 5 and a press release. The London insurance market understood this before most capitals did. When the Joint War Committee extended its Black Sea listed area on September 16, it covered the entire sea except the territorial waters of Bulgaria, Georgia, Romania and Turkey. The underwriters drew the same line the drone operators did. Nobody should find that comforting.

This is what gray zone conflict looks like. Freighters burning off the coasts of two NATO allies, sailors lost in cold water, and attacks clustered around the Sulina Channel, which became the main outlet for Ukrainian grain after Russia hammered Ukraine's own ports. It is war at a time and place of the attacker's choosing, priced just below the point where anyone is obliged to do anything about it.

"The problem is that we cannot prove it"

Bulgaria's prime minister, Rumen Radev, is nobody's idea of a Russia hawk. He told his parliament the logic of the attacks points to Moscow, and then said the quiet part out loud: "The problem is that we cannot prove it."

NATO's response has been built to solve Radev's problem. After the North Atlantic Council met on October 20, the Alliance announced it would send maritime patrol aircraft, radar, drones, intelligence personnel and forensic teams to examine the explosives. A U.S. Navy P-8 Poseidon is already flying the Black Sea. These are sensible deployments. They are also answers to the wrong question.

Play the scenario out. Grant NATO perfect attribution. The forensic teams recover a guidance board with Russian markings. The P-8 tracks a launch back to a known site. The Alliance announces, with high confidence, that the Russian Federation sank the ship. Now make it worse: the next drone hits a tanker alongside the pier at Constanța, the fire spreads, and thousands of civilians are dead.

The Kremlin denies it. Within the hour, Russian state media points at Kyiv, and it doesn't have to work hard to sell the story. Ukraine has been running its own maritime drone campaign since July, so the Black Sea is full of Ukrainian drones, and everyone knows it. A few Western commentators find the denial "plausible enough to warrant caution." Allies invoke Article 4 and consult. Statements are issued. Sanctions, already near their ceiling, are tightened at the margins. Then nothing happens, because every capital in the room is doing the same arithmetic: Russia has nuclear weapons, the Black Sea is not worth a war, and the dead are already dead.

You don't have to imagine that sequence. We ran it on July 17, 2014, when a Buk missile destroyed Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 over eastern Ukraine and killed everyone aboard. A Dutch-led investigation established in 2016 that the launcher had been delivered from Russia, and by 2018 that it came from a Russian army unit. The ICAO Council found Russia responsible in May 2025. The European Court of Human Rights did the same that July. Moscow denied all of it, spent years promoting theories that blamed Ukraine, and in 2022 invaded the country the missile had been fired over. Attribution was as good as attribution gets. The consequence, eleven years later, was an order to enter into good-faith negotiations on reparations.

That is the lesson Moscow took from MH17, and it is the one we refuse to learn. Deniability is not a shield for the attacker. It is a gift to the defender who would rather not act. Russia doesn't need us to believe its denials. It only needs us to want to.

Operational freedom is the target

The point of these strikes isn't the ships. It's the water around them. Every hull that burns off Sulina raises the premium on the next one, pushes a charterer toward a different route, and teaches a shipowner that a NATO coastline offers no protection. The attacker never has to declare a blockade. The market imposes it for him. Freedom of action shrinks by increments, each too small to justify a response, until the defender wakes up to find that the sea he was sure he controlled has a new landlord.

This is how Russia and China will impose costs on the West for the foreseeable future. Not with the decisive battle our doctrine, our budgets, and our military exercises are built around, but with a steady accumulation of incidents chosen for their deniability, timed to our distractions, and calibrated to our fear of escalation. Salami slicing is not a new idea; Beijing has practiced it in the South China Sea for more than a decade. What's new is the drone, which makes the slicing cheap, precise and anonymous.

The honest complication

The Black Sea gray zone is not one-sided, and pretending otherwise hands Moscow its talking points. Ukraine's Operation Molochka, launched in July, claims to have disabled 300 Russian-linked vessels in the Black and Azov Seas. Turkey's foreign minister says both sides are mounting heavy attacks to establish superiority before winter.

The distinction holds. Ukraine is striking the logistics of the country that invaded it, mostly sanctioned tankers serving Russian ports and occupied Crimea. Russia is striking grain ships in the economic zones of two NATO members that are not party to the war, with the apparent aim of making Ukraine's last reliable export route uninsurable. One is a belligerent waging war at sea. The other is exporting that war to the Alliance's doorstep and daring it to notice.

Taiwan won't look like Hellscape

If you want to know what a Taiwan conflict will look like, watch the Black Sea.

In 2024, Adm. Samuel Paparo said he wanted to "turn the Taiwan Strait into an unmanned hellscape" to defeat what he described as Beijing's likely plan: a massive attack with little warning. It's a sound concept, and the CNAS work that fleshed it out this year is serious. Hellscape is built to break an amphibious assault at the water's edge.

Beijing is rehearsing something else. The PLA's Justice Mission 2025 drills in December, run alongside the China Coast Guard, simulated a blockade of Taiwan's main ports and control of the waterways that carry its energy imports. This year the China Coast Guard and Maritime Safety Administration have run what the Jamestown Foundation calls a "quasi-quarantine" east of the island, creating the appearance of administrative control without declaring a blockade. Taiwan has already prosecuted a Chinese captain for severing an undersea cable. Each step is a law enforcement action, an inspection, an accident. None of them is an invasion.

A drone swarm waiting in the Strait for a landing force has nothing to shoot at when the adversary is a coast guard cutter boarding a container ship for a "safety inspection." The first Taiwanese or American drone to fire makes Taipei the aggressor. So Beijing won't cross the Strait. It will tighten the noose: a quarantine, a severed cable, an insurance listing, a shipping line that quietly decides Kaohsiung isn't worth the premium. It will bank on the world's risk aversion. It’s already working. After the May summit in Beijing, Washington paused a record $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, and the President described those sales as a "very good negotiating chip". Taiwan will not be conquered. It will be persuaded, one closed option at a time, that there is nothing left to defend.

Answering below the threshold

You cannot deter gray zone coercion with a capability designed for the war the adversary is careful never to start. The answer has to live in the same band the attacker does: below the threshold of general war, above the threshold of pain. Three steps would help in the Black Sea, and each has a Pacific twin.

Presence that denies, not presence that watches. Turkey, Romania and Bulgaria already run a Mine Countermeasures Task Group whose mandate was widened in July to cover undersea infrastructure. Montreux restricts warships of non-Black Sea states, not the littoral navies. Widen the mandate once more, to counter-drone escort of merchant traffic through allied economic zones, and buy the equipment from the Ukrainians who have kept their own grain corridor open under fire. In the Pacific, the equivalent is a convoy and escort plan for a quarantine, not only a kill chain for an invasion.

Decide the response before the incident. The moment of decision is where risk aversion wins, because it is always easier to wait for one more forensic report. Allies should agree in advance, and say publicly, what a verified strike on shipping in their waters will cost Moscow: a pre-approved tranche of capability released to Ukraine, a pre-agreed number of shadow fleet hulls detained. Attribution should trigger an equivalent consequence, not another discussion. Taipei and Washington need the same menu for a quarantine, written now, while no one is under pressure.

Take the market off the adversary's side. When insurers and charterers do the attacker's work, governments need a sovereign war-risk backstop for vessels trading to allied ports, so the next listed-area extension doesn't function as a blockade by spreadsheet. Taiwan will need that backstop on the first day of a quarantine, not the ninetieth.

None of this is escalation. It is the minimum required to make the gray zone cost something.

The Thirteenth Mile

The Khoryv went down one mile outside a line we drew. The adversary picked the mile. Next time it will pick the hour, the cargo, the flag and the ocean. The question for the Alliance isn't whether we can prove who did it. It's whether, once we prove it, we will do anything.

item.title: The Intelligence Community’s Missing Discipline
item.description:
Economic statecraft has become a primary instrument of US national security, deployed with a frequency and ambition that outpaces the intelligence architecture built to support it. For sanctions, tariffs, investment screening, export controls, and development finance to succeed, the United States must fully leverage the data and intelligence available to it. Now is the time for the IC to organize itself around the discipline of economic and financial intelligence.

The IC has long struggled to prove its value to economic customers: the Secretaries of Treasury, Commerce, Defense, and State, as well as the US Trade Representative and financial regulators. One frequent explanation is the IC’s historic orientation toward military and diplomatic support. Another is the perception that classified economic analysis lacks distinctive value. I spent most of a twenty-three-year intelligence career inside the economic discipline, ultimately leading Treasury’s Office of Intelligence and Analysis (OIA). While this may once have been true, the IC is doing better than ever to meet growing demand.

The problem is no longer the quality of the analysis—which has matured immensely—but the IC’s decentralized approach to serving its economic customers. No IC agency is specifically responsible for the discipline of economic and financial intelligence. The closest is OIA.

Congress created OIA in statute in 2004 with an eye toward sanctions support and countering terrorism finance. Its role has since expanded across economic, financial, and cyber issues for customers across government and industry. However, OIA is not the designated IC lead for US economic statecraft—no IC agency is. One consequence is that the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) remains the statutory lead for analytic support to the Treasury-led Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS). That made sense in 2007, when the Foreign Investment and National Security Act codified CFIUS and assigned the Director of National Intelligence that role. At the time, OIA was in its infancy and consumed by counterterrorism. That is no longer the case.

The instinct in Washington is to solve a challenge like this by first creating a new organization, then fixing the functions. Congress should start with the functions instead, then address where the discipline sits. To improve IC support to economic statecraft, Congress must first act on six fronts.

Designate a functional manager. One IC element must own economic and financial intelligence as a discipline: collection priorities, analytic standards, a hiring and training pipeline, and a framework for systematic engagement with allies and industry. Nothing about that role requires a new agency.

Clarify authorities. Explicitly authorize collaboration between the designated lead and both its government customers and the private sector, including exchange of expertise and data.

Supercharge private sector engagement. Many of the best national security solutions in economics and finance will come from industry. Create a permanent path for its ideas, expertise, and capabilities.

Work with what exists. Use OIA as the foundation and keep the number of IC agencies flat, but cap its size so it stays nimble as economic statecraft evolves.

Revisit ODNI’s CFIUS role. IC support to CFIUS sits with ODNI because in 2007 no one else could carry it. Whether it should move depends on where the discipline lands, but Congress should not view the 2007 answer as permanent.

Fund it as a national mission. Economic intelligence should not have to compete for a share of a domestic department’s topline. Give the discipline a dedicated budget line, with the investment in people and AI that exploiting economic data at scale requires.

That leaves where the discipline sits—and there are three answers, not one.

The easiest first step is a designation: name OIA the functional manager, leave it in Treasury, and make clear in statute and to policy customers that OIA is the center of gravity for economic and financial intelligence. That is available now and beats the status quo. Nevertheless, an IC office answering to the Secretary of the Treasury will always be seen—correctly—as Treasury’s first. This is why Commerce and others periodically press for shops of their own, an outcome that grows the IC rather than optimizing it.

The achievable reform is bureau status. Treasury did this with FinCEN in 2002, and FinCEN is now treated as a government-wide and international resource rather than Treasury’s alone. Done properly it means a separate appropriation, a director accountable to both the Secretary and the DNI, and a statutory mission naming service to the whole government, the private sector, and our allies.

The stretch option is to elevate OIA to become an independent National Geo-Economic Intelligence Agency—still my own preference, because only independence settles the question of whose intelligence office it is. But where the discipline sits is the last decision, not the first. Under any of the three, the proximity OIA has built with Treasury policymakers is a design problem with a known solution: dedicated, co-located teams at each major customer department.

Economic intelligence is a core national security capability and should be organized and resourced like one: purpose-built to track, anticipate, and disrupt adversary financial and commercial threats in real time. The playbook has changed. Our competitors are more agile, emboldened, and shaping markets and supply chains to their advantage while we debate whether the threat qualifies as strategic.

item.title: We’re Losing the Cognitive Space Race
item.description:
Over the last century, modern medicine achieved a historic feat. We increased the human lifespan by 33%. But at the same time, we completely failed to defend our brain healthspan. Today, a silent gap of 15 to 30 years exists between the time our bodies survive and the time our brains remain vibrant, innovative, and fully functional. It is a terrifying paradox. Medical science has advanced so much that a newborn today can realistically expect to live to 100, if not 120 years old. Yet, we passively accept that their cognitive engine will begin an irreversible, downhill slide in their thirties with the likelihood of dementia reaching almost 100% by the age of 110. What good is an extra three decades of biological existence if our brains lack the strength and resilience to enjoy it? This is no longer just a localized healthcare crisis; it is an imminent national security threat to our competitive edge.

Look at where our national focus and funding are directed. America is focused on investing billions of dollars into artificial intelligence and hypersonic defense systems. However, we are systematically ignoring the ultimate computing engine that builds the technology, commands our military, drives our economy, and stabilizes our communities: the human brain.

Our global competitors are not making this mistake. Most notably, China understands that future geopolitical dominance will not be won simply by hoarding raw technology. It will be won by the cognitive longevity, relentless innovation, and emotional resilience of their population. They are playing the long game and investing in their brain economy; We are falling behind.

In the military, we use a concept called staying "left of boom." It means executing proactive, aggressive conditioning and preventative strategies to stop a catastrophe before it happens, rather than digging through the wreckage after an explosion.

Right now, America’s approach to brain health is reactive. Our public policy treats brain aging as an inevitable, downhill slide into deficit. We pour billions of dollars into solving brain health collapse, like dementia and visible cognitive breakdown, before we actively intervene. But that approach is a losing strategy. We must shift from a reactive, disease-focused model to a proactive era of precision brain health in order to finally maximize American brainpower. If we do not actively optimize our collective intelligence and mental endurance, we will fall behind not only in defense readiness but also in scientific advancement and workforce productivity.

Fortunately, building a sharper, more resilient nation has never been easier or more measurable.

A landmark, three-year longitudinal study of 4,000 adults recently published in Nature Portfolio’s Scientific Reports completely dismantles the myth of inevitable cognitive decline. The data proves that the human brain possesses a no-ceiling capability. From ages 19 to 94, the brain retains a profound capacity to continually rewire, adapt, and improve its performance over time.

The key to unlocking this potential is a newly validated, multidimensional metric called the BrainHealth Index. For the first time, we can treat the brain exactly like physical fitness. We don't guess if our hearts are healthy; we measure blood pressure. The BrainHealth Index finally gives us a credible benchmark to track and measure holistic brain improvement across three critical pillars:

  • Clarity: Our raw capacity to solve complex, novel problems and drive deep technological innovation.
  • Connectedness: Our capacity for social purpose and communication, which serves as the bedrock for stable families and strong communities.
  • Emotional Balance: The mental resilience required to perform under extreme pressure, from corporate boardrooms to tactical defense environments.

When we actively invest in and train our cognitive micro-skills, the positive implications ripple across society. Every day, citizens become better in their personal relationships, more productive at their jobs, and significantly more resilient against modern burnout and life stressors. Scaled nationally, this collective mental fitness becomes the invisible armor required for our national defense and technological endurance.

As a neurologist, a retired U.S. Army Colonel, and the former founding director of DARPA’s Biological Technologies Office, I have spent my entire career protecting and restoring the brains of our service members. I know what the human mind is capable of achieving when it is pushed to optimize, rather than just manage decline.

Our federal agencies, including the Department of Health and Human Services, the NIH, and the Department of Veterans Affairs, must immediately work to adopt scalable, digital health initiatives that democratize these brain optimization tools nationwide. But executive action is only half the battle. Congress must step up and introduce a unified, bipartisan National Brain Capital Act. Just as lawmakers realized we could not secure our future without a CHIPS and Science Act to defend our artificial intelligence hardware, they must recognize that we cannot protect our nation without a legislative framework to maximize our human brainpower. We must empower every single citizen with the self-agency to improve their own cognitive capacity. It is time for Congress to stop treating brain performance as a passive medical luxury for the few. It is a national imperative to keep America leading the world.

item.description:
